overview: Zip Co is a Sydney-headquartered digital financial services company offering point-of-sale credit (Buy Now Pay Later, or 'Pay-in-Z') and digital payment products, connecting millions of customers with tens of thousands of merchants. Founded in 2013, Zip now operates in two core markets — Australia/New Zealand (ANZ, with NZ being wound down from July 2026) and the United States (its largest growth market) — after divesting loss-making UK, European (Twisto) and Middle Eastern (Spotii) operations in 2022-23. The company has completed a multi-year turnaround from large statutory losses (FY22: ~A$1.02bn loss; FY23: ~A$401m loss) to record profitability in FY26 (cash EBTDA of A$268.9m, statutory NPAT of A$116.4m).

business_model.summary: Zip earns a merchant fee (percentage of transaction value) plus, in some products, customer-paid fees (late fees in ANZ under a capped, regulated fee structure; account/service fees and, in longer-duration US products, interest-like charges) on point-of-sale instalment credit. Revenue is transactional/volume-driven (tied to Total Transaction Volume, or TTV) rather than subscription-based, though repeat usage by an engaged active-customer base gives it recurring characteristics. The core unit-economics driver is 'cash NTM' (net transaction margin) — TTV/revenue less funding costs and net bad debts — which management then leverages via largely fixed opex to generate cash EBTDA.

revenue_streams.name: ANZ segment revenue (BNPL, Zip Plus, ZMobile)

business_model.customer_type: B2C consumer credit with a two-sided platform model (both customers and merchants); merchants range from SMBs to large enterprise (Temu, Samsung, The Iconic, JD Sports, Optimum) accessed increasingly via channel/embedded-finance partners (Stripe, Google Pay/Wallet)
business_model.geographic_mix: US ~59% of FY26 group revenue (A$903.1m AUD-equivalent of A$1,336m group revenue), Australia/NZ ~41% (A$432.9m); New Zealand operations being wound down from July 2026 to concentrate on Australia and the US

main_competitors: bank-led BNPL (CommBank StepPay, NAB Now Pay Later)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the two dominant BNPL providers in Australia (alongside Afterpay/Block) with ~1.9m ANZ active customers (~10% of the Australian adult population) and 6.6% AU household penetration claims; in the US, an early-stage but fast-growing challenger (4.6m active customers, 30.8k merchants) behind larger-scale peers Affirm and Klarna but differentiated by underwriting under-served low-to-middle income consumers

moat_factors.description: Differentiated ability to credit-decision low-to-middle income and thin-file US consumers profitably; short-duration, low-AOV portfolio (US AOV ~US$141) keeps losses low (net bad debts 1.7% of TTV, within 1.5-2.0% target)
97.4k total merchants and 6.5m active customers create mutual reinforcement, though merchant multi-homing across BNPL providers is common and limits exclusivity
General availability across all Stripe US merchants, Google Pay/Wallet and Chrome Autofill integrations provide low-cost, capital-light customer/merchant acquisition
High NPS scores (+72 US, +76 ANZ) and long operating history (13 years) versus newer entrants

From 10 June 2025 all Australian BNPL providers require an ASIC credit licence and must run credit checks, raising compliance costs and creating a barrier against unlicensed new entrants — benefits incumbents like Zip and Afterpay who have already built compliance infrastructure

weaknesses: Smaller scale than Affirm and Klarna in the US, and smaller than Block/Afterpay group-wide, limiting funding-cost and negotiating leverage with merchants
No pricing power over consumers in AU (fee caps under NCCP regime) and thin net transaction margins mean profitability depends heavily on funding-cost discipline and bad-debt control
Merchant relationships are largely non-exclusive; retailers can and do offer multiple BNPL options simultaneously
History of capital-destructive, poorly-integrated overseas M&A (QuadPay, Twisto, Spotii, UK) that had to be unwound at large impairment cost

growth_drivers: US TTV/revenue growth (42.5%/44.3% in FY26, USD) — FY27 guidance of at least 30% US TTV growth — in a market of 100m+ Americans management views as underserved by traditional credit
Product innovation: Pay-in-2 (launched Feb 2026, +86% QoQ transactions in 4Q26) targeting non-discretionary spend (groceries, utilities), and scaling of Pay-in-8 and 'My Bills'

New capital-light adjacent products: ZMobile (Australian mobile plans, launched May 2026) and embedded finance/agentic commerce partnerships (Google, Stripe, Visa, IXOPAY) positioning Zip for AI-driven checkout

ANZ reacceleration: revenue and AU receivables returned to growth (+4.6%/+9.4%) after several flat years, aided by Zip Plus higher credit limits and new enterprise merchants (Samsung, The Iconic, Expedia)
Continued operating leverage/margin expansion (FY26 group operating margin +420bps to 20.0%; FY27 guided to 20-22%) as fixed cost base is spread over a larger TTV base
Funding cost reduction via a diversified, larger funding platform (new US$283.4m two-year US warehouse facility, October 2025) and zero corporate debt
Potential Nasdaq dual listing under consideration to access US capital markets and raise investor visibility in its largest growth market
AI/automation initiatives (100% of staff using enterprise AI tools, 86% of code AI-assisted) supporting further opex efficiency

business.description: Crowded BNPL/instalment-credit landscape with Affirm, Klarna, Afterpay/Block, Sezzle, PayPal, and bank-native products (CommBank StepPay, NAB Now Pay Later) competing for merchants and prime consumers, pressuring merchant fee rates and customer acquisition costs
Core customer base skews to low-to-middle income, credit-constrained consumers who are more exposed to cost-of-living and employment shocks
July 2026 announced wind-down of NZ operations carries near-term execution/customer-transition costs, though strategically refocuses capital on higher-return AU/US markets
Prior UK, Twisto (Czech) and Spotii (UAE) acquisitions were impaired and divested at significant loss; execution risk exists if Zip re-enters M&A as part of US scale-up

financial.description: As an unsecured consumer lender, Zip is exposed to net bad debts (managed within 1.5-2.0% of TTV target in the US); a downturn in consumer credit quality would compress margins

financial.risk: Funding cost and warehouse facility renewal risk
financial.description: Zip relies on securitised warehouse funding facilities (e.g., new US$283.4m 2-year facility, AU Master Trust and 2017-1 Trust); higher-for-longer interest rates raise funding costs and facilities must be periodically refinanced/renewed
US dollar earnings translated to AUD reporting currency create translation volatility; ~59% of group revenue is USD-denominated
Company has no dividend policy; Equity Incentive Plan allocations create dilution, partially offset by share buybacks (A$150m completed FY26) and on-market ESP purchases

regulatory.description: From 10 June 2025, all Australian BNPL providers must hold an ASIC credit licence and conduct credit checks under a new Low Cost Credit Contract framework, raising compliance costs and altering underwriting/product design; while a barrier to new entrants, ongoing regulatory changes could further cap fees or restrict product features
BNPL remains an evolving regulatory area in the US (state licensing, potential federal disclosure/interest-rate rules); increased scrutiny could raise compliance costs or constrain product economics
Regulators and consumer advocacy groups continue to scrutinise BNPL affordability assessments and hardship handling, a persistent reputational and compliance risk

macro.description: Cost-of-living pressures and weaker labour markets in Australia/US could reduce discretionary TTV and raise delinquencies, even though management notes growing share from non-discretionary categories (groceries, utilities, health)
Higher-for-longer rates raise the cost of warehouse/securitised funding, compressing net transaction margins unless offset by repricing or portfolio mix shift

macro.risk: Macroeconomic/credit cycle risk in the US
macro.description: US expansion is core to the growth thesis; a US recession or credit tightening cycle would disproportionately affect the newer, higher-growth US loan book

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Australian BNPL/alternative lending markets are forecast to keep growing at double-digit rates (Australia's BNPL market projected to grow ~15.6% YoY to ~US$18bn in 2026; broader Australian alternative lending market projected to reach ~A$33.6bn by 2029), even as the sector matures and consolidates around a smaller number of well-capitalised players amid tighter regulation
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — BNPL TTV and credit quality are sensitive to consumer discretionary spending and employment conditions, though Zip has deliberately shifted mix toward non-discretionary categories (groceries, utilities, health, insurance) to reduce cyclicality
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — Zip funds its receivables book via warehouse/securitisation facilities, so funding costs move with base rates; management notes positioning for a 'higher for longer' rate environment via funding diversification and repricing
key_input_costs: Cost of funds / interest on warehouse and securitisation facilities

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: record group cash EBTDA of A$268.9m (+57.9% YoY), beating the company's own guidance of at least A$260m; statutory NPAT up 45.7% to A$116.4m; group operating margin expanded 420bps to 20.0%; shares surged ~12-17% on the result
FY27 guidance issued: group cash EBTDA target of A$340m (+26% YoY), operating margin of 20-22%, and US TTV growth of at least 30% (USD terms)
Announced orderly wind-down of New Zealand operations to focus capital on Australia and US growth markets
Established new US$283.4m two-year US warehouse funding facility with two funding partners, improving funding capacity and cost

Achieved general availability across all Stripe US merchants, adding 5,200+ merchants via the partnership since; also completed A$150m on-market share buyback in FY26 and secured proprietary ownership of the Zip trademark in Australia

Board reported to be actively assessing a potential Nasdaq dual listing to support US growth and access US capital markets, with CEO Cynthia Scott relocating to the US to align executive leadership with the largest growth market
Launched Pay-in-2 in the US targeting high-frequency, non-discretionary spend (groceries, utilities); transactions grew 86% QoQ by 4Q26
Launched ZMobile in Australia, a capital-light mobile-plan product for existing customers

items.notes: Represents ~26% growth on FY26's record A$268.9m, which itself beat the prior guidance of 'at least A$260m'
FY26 achieved 20.0% (up 420bps YoY); FY27 range implies continued expansion at the top end
FY26 US TTV grew 42.5% in USD; FY27 guide of 'at least 30%' implies continued strong but moderating growth off a larger base
FY26 came in at 1.7% of TTV, within the target range, as Pay-in-8/Pay-in-2 scale

items.target: Continue optimising capital structure; no corporate debt
items.notes: Nil corporate debt at FY26 year-end; completed A$150m buyback in FY26; further capital-return/optimisation flagged as a FY27 strategic priority

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Diane Smith-Gander and Group CEO Cynthia Scott characterised FY26 as reflecting 'a stronger, more resilient business' built on operating leverage, a diversified funding platform and disciplined risk management. Management framed FY27 priorities around two pillars: 'Drive growth and innovation' (compounding core-business growth, new product segments, AI-enabled customer experiences) and 'Invest for long-term scale' (platform investment, AI acceleration, continued capital structure optimisation). The Board said it remains committed to 'fit-for-purpose regulation' and will only proceed with a potential US dual listing 'when we believe it is in the best interests of all shareholders.'

bull_case: Genuine turnaround story: from a ~A$1.02bn FY22 loss and near-death experience to 12 consecutive quarters of group profitability, record FY26 cash EBTDA (+58%) and statutory NPAT (+46%), with no corporate debt

US business is a large, still-early-stage growth opportunity (4.6m of 100m+ underserved Americans, TTV +42.5% in FY26) with improving unit economics (operating margin 25.0%, +113bps) and expanding embedded-finance distribution via Stripe, Google and Visa

Significant operating leverage remaining: group operating margin expanded 420bps to 20.0% in FY26 and is guided to 20-22% in FY27, meaning incremental TTV should continue to convert disproportionately to cash earnings

Diversified, capital-light growth optionality via new products (Pay-in-2, ZMobile) and agentic-commerce partnerships positions Zip for a potential re-rating as an AI-enabled fintech platform rather than a pure BNPL name
Capital return underway (A$150m buyback completed FY26) alongside strategic options (potential Nasdaq listing) to access lower-cost US capital and improve valuation/liquidity
bear_case: Crowded, commoditising competitive landscape (Afterpay/Block, Klarna, Affirm, Sezzle, PayPal, and bank-native instalment products) limits Zip's pricing power and could compress merchant fee take-rates over time
Post-June-2025 Australian credit licensing/NCCP regime raises compliance costs and could further constrain product design or fees; ongoing US regulatory attention to BNPL adds uncertainty

US growth is funded by a credit book serving predominantly low-to-middle income, credit-constrained consumers — a segment historically more vulnerable to interest-rate and employment shocks, testing underwriting discipline as the book scales
Reliance on securitised warehouse funding facilities exposes margins to funding-cost inflation in a higher-for-longer rate environment, and facilities require periodic renewal

Track record includes value-destructive prior international expansion (UK, Twisto, Spotii) written off at large impairment cost; execution risk remains if the company pursues US scale-up aggressively (including any Nasdaq listing) without disciplined capital allocation
